query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Repetitive mechanical disruption of the passive film, combined with the alloy’s ability or inability to rapidly re-passivate, governs the total tribo-corrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys. When the removal of the film outpaces the re-growth (due to high mechanical load and/or slow re-passivation), both wear and corrosion rates increase synergistically.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy initially exhibiting stable passivation film and moderate hardness in a chloride-containing environment.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary normal load (e.g., 5–30 N), sliding speed (e.g., 1–10 mm/s), and electrochemical potential in a single tribo-corrosion cell. Monitor real-time friction, mass loss, electrochemical currents, and the re-passivation behavior, and compare to no-load corrosion tests (pure corrosion) and inert-environment sliding tests (pure wear).
generation.conditions: Tests performed at controlled temperature, with a 3.5 wt% NaCl electrolyte, measuring both wear track topography and electrochemical signals across different mechanical and electrochemical conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Protective oxide or passive layer at the surface, which, when continuously disrupted by mechanical contact, modifies local corrosion kinetics via de-passivation and re-passivation cycles.
generation.mechanism: The competing effects of passivation and mechanical removal control overall damage. High mechanical loads or contact pressures cause frequent film breakdown, whereas rapid oxide re-growth limits corrosion in between sliding events. The balance between the disruption rate and re-passivation kinetics determines the extent of synergistic wear–corrosion damage.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under higher loads and faster sliding speeds, total mass loss will exceed the sum of pure corrosion and pure wear losses, demonstrating synergy. Enhancing re-passivation kinetics (e.g., via favorable alloy composition or environment) will decrease this synergy and reduce overall tribo-corrosion.
generation.baseline: Material behavior under separate pure corrosion and pure wear conditions, where no synergy between mechanical removal and film breakdown occurs. Total damage under combined tribo-corrosion should exceed this sum if the hypothesis holds.
generation.boundary: In extremely inert environments or under very low loads where mechanical disruption is minimal, passivation breakdown and synergy should be negligible. Conversely, at very high loads or in extremely aggressive solutions, other mechanisms (e.g., large-scale plastic deformation or localized corrosion) may become dominant.
generation.uncertainty: Localized microcracking, variable microstructure, or variations in alloy composition could alter repassivation responses and confound the predicted synergy.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct tribo-corrosion tests while actively modifying re-passivation kinetics (e.g., doping the electrolyte to accelerate or impede oxide film formation), at fixed mechanical loads and sliding speeds, while comparing total damage with pure wear and corrosion controls.
measurements: Mass loss and wear track depth metrics
Time-resolved characterization of film breakdown and reformation (e.g., via electrochemical impedance or surface imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If altering the speed of film re-passivation does not significantly change measured synergy (i.e., total damage remains the same regardless of how quickly or slowly the film reforms), then the hypothesis that re-passivation kinetics governs tribo-corrosion is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

AbstractThe challenge of cavitation erosion (CE) in flow-handling components of marine engineering has promoted the development of advanced materials due to safety incidents and economic costs. High entropy alloys (HEAs), known for high hardness and corrosion resistance, emerge as promising candidates. This paper delved into the CE characteristics of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA when subjected to the 3.5 wt% NaCl solution, elucidating the synergistic effect of CE-corrosion. The quantitative analysis revealed that CE-corrosion synergy contributed 48.02% to total CE mass loss, primarily attributed to corrosion-induced CE damage. Meanwhile, electrochemical noise (EN) was utilized to reveal the corrosion behavior of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution combined with the morphologies observation and surface roughness. Extended CE time compromised the corrosion resistance of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA and diminished the impact of selective phase corrosion on the surface. Eventually, the CE damage mechanism of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA was revealed based on pertinent experimental findings. Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. While recent publications have presented experimental evidence of low friction or high wear resistance (but typically not both) with HEAs, they were performed in environments where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films was prevalent. These phenomena can greatly impact strength and deformation/wear resistance. decision.trend: Recent work on high-entropy alloys under combined mechanical and corrosive conditions (tribo-corrosion, cavitation erosion-corrosion, friction-corrosion) highlights promising but incomplete insights on how their protective films and microstructure evolve under simultaneous wear and chemical attack. Early efforts focused on separate wear or corrosion tests, while newer studies examine the synergy directly by combining friction/corrosion or cavitation/corrosion. These report beneficial roles of stable passivation films and robust microstructures in mitigating degradation, yet results vary with temperature, microstructure, environmental chemistry, and mechanical loading. Despite progress, the fundamental interplay of wear-assisted depassivation, re-passivation kinetics, and possible mechanical activation of localized corrosion remains only partially understood.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear whether the dominant factor controlling tribo-corrosion in high-entropy alloys is (1) the repeated mechanical disruption of protective surface films, (2) the capacity for rapid re-passivation, or (3) the local mechanical alteration of the near-surface microstructure that accelerates corrosion—including how differences in alloy structural stability affect these processes.
decision.lever: Vary normal load, sliding speed, and applied electrochemical potential while measuring in situ friction, mass loss, and electrochemical response in a single tribo-corrosion cell, then compare with pure wear-only and pure corrosion-only baselines. Specifically, track how quickly and uniformly the protective oxide film reforms after mechanical disruption, using surface-sensitive techniques (e.g., real-time electrochemical impedance) to discern relative contributions of mechanical depassivation and re-passivation kinetics.
decision.why: Because prior research traces coupled wear-corrosion damage to the breakdown of passive films and the synergy between mechanical disruption and corrosion, a controlled experiment that systematically varies mechanical and electrochemical parameters simultaneously can directly isolate the role of repassivation kinetics as the governing mechanism. Demonstration that enhanced or impeded film regrowth strongly modulates total degradation (and that these changes track with both friction data and electrochemical signals) would confirm the hypothesis. Conversely, if altering repassivation rates does not significantly modify total tribo-corrosion, that result would falsify the proposed explanation.
